alambic.intro: The sun evaporates moisture from the soil and plants, which condenses under plastic and runs into a container. Low yield: keep it for dry, sunny regions.
etapes: Dig a hole about 90 cm wide and 60 cm deep, in a sunny, damp spot (valley bottom, wet ground).
Put a container in the centre of the hole, and line the edge with cut green non-poisonous plants.
Cover the hole with a clear plastic sheet, edges buried so it's airtight.
Put a small pebble in the middle of the sheet, just above the container, to form a cone.
Wait: drops run to the tip of the cone and fall into the container. Collect in the evening without lifting the sheet if possible (a tube helps).
attention: Yield of 0.3 to 0.6 litres a day, for a lot of effort: in temperate areas, rain is almost always a better option.
Never poisonous plants in the hole.
alambic.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

pierres_chaudes.intro: Stones heated in the fire and dropped into water can boil it in any container that can't go on the fire.
etapes: Gather dry stones the size of an egg or a fist, away from water (never river pebbles).
Heat them in the heart of the fire for at least 30 minutes.
Prepare the container: plastic bottle or mess tin, wooden bowl, or a hole in the ground lined with a tarp.
Pick up a stone with two sticks used as tongs, shake off the ash, drop it into the water.
Add the stones one by one until there is a rolling boil, and keep it for 1 minute.
attention: Damp or porous stones can burst: keep your distance from the fire and protect your eyes.
Then strain the water through a cloth to remove the ash.
pierres_chaudes.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

cold.titre: The COLD rule for staying warm
cold.intro: Four principles from military cold-weather manuals, valid whenever it's cool and damp.
etapes: C for Clean: dirty, greasy clothes insulate poorly, because dirt crushes the air pockets that hold warmth.
O for avoid Overheating: open your jacket, take off a layer, remove hat or gloves as soon as effort makes you sweat. Sweat wets clothing and chills you as it dries.
L for Loose and Layered: clothes that are too tight cut off circulation. Several thin layers beat one thick one, thanks to the air trapped between them.
D for Dry: protect your clothes from rain and snow, dry them as soon as possible. Damp socks dry against your body or on your pack while you walk.
attention: Never dry leather boots too close to the fire: they harden and crack.
cold.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

riviere.intro: River crossings are among the most serious hiking accidents. The best decision is often not to cross.
etapes: Don't cross if the water is fast and above the knees, very cold, murky (you can't see the bottom) or in flood.
Look for the right spot from a high point: where the river is wide and splits into several channels, shallow, without slippery rocks, upstream of a sand or gravel bar.
Avoid rapids, rock steps, the area near a waterfall and the eddies behind large obstacles.
Keep your shoes on, undo the pack's hip belt and chest strap so you can get rid of it.
Cross facing the current, leaning on a strong stick placed upstream (three points of support), moving diagonally downstream.
In a group: stand shoulder to shoulder in a line in the direction of the current, the strongest upstream.
Dry and warm your feet and legs immediately on the other side.
attention: If you're swept away: on your back, feet first at the surface to cushion against rocks, and swim diagonally towards the bank. Never try to stand up in a strong current (risk of trapping a foot).
riviere.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

pas.intro: Without GPS, knowing how many metres you've covered lets you locate yourself on the map.
etapes: Calibrate before you go: walk a measured 100 m counting one step each time your left foot touches the ground (a “double step”).
Most adults take 60 to 70 double steps per 100 m on flat ground. Note your number.
While walking, tie a knot in a cord or move a pebble from one pocket to the other every 100 m.
Adjust for the terrain: you take more steps uphill, on steep descents, in vegetation, snow or at night.
pas.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

recoupement.intro: With a map, a compass and two visible landmarks, you can find your exact position.
etapes: Pick two clearly visible features that are easy to find on the map (summit, pylon, church tower, end of a lake), ideally 60 to 90° apart.
Aim at the first with the compass and read its angle (bearing).
Work out the back bearing: add 180° if it's less than 180°, otherwise subtract 180°.
On the map, draw a line from that landmark in the direction of the back bearing.
Do the same with the second landmark: you are where the two lines cross.
Simpler: if you're on a known path or river, one bearing is enough, as you are where the line meets the path.
recoupement.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

navigation.intro: Four simple techniques so you don't miss your destination.
etapes: The handrail: follow a linear feature (path, river, forest edge, power line) that leads near the goal, rather than cutting through the woods.
Aiming off: to reach a bridge over a river, deliberately aim a little to the left. When you reach the river, you know you need to turn right.
The attack point: start from an obvious, nearby landmark (junction, end of a lake) to find a discreet goal (a spring, a bivouac area).
The catching feature: find on the map a feature just beyond the goal (stream, road). If you reach it, you've gone too far.
navigation.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

miroir.intro: In sunshine, a mirror is the best way to be seen from afar: a flash can be spotted dozens of kilometres away.
etapes: Without a mirror: the phone screen, a CD, a survival blanket, the polished bottom of a mess tin.
Stretch your free arm out in front of you, fingers in a V, and place the plane or helicopter between the two fingers.
With the other hand, angle the mirror so the patch of sunlight falls on your outstretched hand.
Gently and rhythmically tilt the mirror to sweep the reflection from your hand to the target, then back.
Climb to a high point if possible, and aim towards the sound if you can't see the aircraft.
attention: Don't flash very fast, and don't keep the reflection on the cockpit for more than a few seconds: you'd dazzle the pilot.
miroir.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

solair.intro: Five symbols understood by all air rescue services, to mark on the ground in an open area.
etapes: V: need help.
X: need medical assistance.
N: no.
Y: yes.
Arrow: I'm leaving in this direction.
Size: at least 4 m wide by 6 m long (2:3 ratio), with strokes about 1 m wide.
Materials: branches, stones, clothing, survival blanket, trampled grass or packed snow. The symbol must contrast with the ground: straight lines and sharp angles don't exist in nature and stand out.
solair.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

cordelette.intro: Long nettle stems and the inner bark of the lime tree give strong fibres. The “reverse twist” technique turns them into cord.
etapes: Cut tall nettle stems in late summer or autumn (with gloves), and strip the leaves.
Crush each stem flat along its whole length, open it and remove the woody core: you're left with a strip of fibres.
Let the fibres dry a little, then soften them between your fingers.
Fold a bundle of fibres in two, not quite in the middle. Hold the fold in your left hand.
Twist the upper strand towards you, then cross it over the other, away from you. Repeat with the new upper strand.
Add new fibres before the end of each strand, staggered, to lengthen the cord.
Test the strength by pulling hard and tying a knot: if it doesn't break, the cord is usable.
attention: Only cut what you need, and never take bark from a living tree.
cordelette.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

ps_pls.intro: For an unconscious person who is breathing: on their side, their tongue no longer blocks the throat and they won't choke if they vomit.
etapes: Check that they don't respond but are breathing normally (watch the belly rise, listen, feel the breath for 10 seconds).
If they're not breathing or breathing abnormally: call 112 and start chest compressions if you're trained.
Place the arm nearest you at a right angle, palm up.
Put the back of their other hand against their cheek, on your side, and hold it there.
Raise their far knee, foot on the ground, and pull on that knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
Adjust the upper leg to a right angle and tilt the head back slightly, mouth towards the ground.
Call 112, cover the person and check their breathing regularly until help arrives.
attention: After a serious fall with suspected neck injury, only move them if they risk choking or the place is dangerous.
isole: Put the person in the recovery position (steps below in Help reachable mode) and stay close to them.
Check their breathing every 2 to 3 minutes at first, then regularly.
Insulate them from the ground (pack, mat, branches) and cover them: an unconscious person cools down very quickly.
Every 30 minutes, turn them onto the other side to avoid pressure injuries.
Note the time, their breathing and their responses: these notes will help the rescuers.
If they stop breathing: lay them on their back and start chest compressions (30 compressions in the centre of the chest, 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute).
alerte: Irregular, noisy breathing or breathing that stops
attentionIsole: Alone and with no help, prolonged CPR has very little chance of success, except after drowning, lightning or hypothermia. Keep going for at least 30 minutes if you can.
ps_pls.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ERC) cross-checked with manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_choc.intro: After a haemorrhage, an extensive burn, a fracture or a severe allergic reaction, the body may no longer supply the organs properly with blood. It is a life-threatening emergency.
etapes: Recognise the signs: pale, cold and clammy skin, fast and weak pulse, fast breathing, thirst, anxiety, weakness, then confusion.
Treat the cause if possible (stop bleeding with pressure).
Lay the casualty on their back, insulate them from the ground, cover them.
If there's no injury to the legs, pelvis or back: raise their legs about 30 cm.
Give them nothing to drink or eat, talk to them, reassure them.
Call 112 and monitor their breathing continuously.
attention: A casualty in shock can deteriorate very quickly: never leave them alone if you can help it.
isole: Stop the cause if possible: pressure on the bleeding, cooling a burn.
Lay them on their back, insulate from the ground and cover. Raise the legs about 30 cm if they're not injured.
Build a shelter against wind and rain over the casualty.
Every 15 minutes: count the pulse and breathing and write them down (Monitoring a casualty sheet).
If they're fully awake, with no belly injury and no vomiting: small sips of water. Otherwise, nothing by mouth.
Don't leave them alone if there are several of you.
alerte: Shock on its own is a warning sign: do everything to get out or be found
ps_choc.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ERC) cross-checked with manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_attelle.intro: With a fracture or a bad sprain, immobilising the limb limits pain and damage while waiting or during transport.
etapes: Don't try to put a bone or joint back in place: immobilise it in the position found.
Prepare two rigid splints (sticks, walking poles, rolled foam mat, cardboard) long enough to block the joint above AND below the injury.
Pad with clothing, especially at bony points (ankles, knees, wrists).
Tie with bandages, scarves or cord, above and below the injury, never directly on it.
Arm: after the splint, support the bent forearm in a sling (jacket, scarf) against the body.
Check every 15 minutes that fingers or toes stay warm, pink and have feeling: if not, loosen.
attention: Open fracture (bone visible): cover the wound with a clean cloth without pressing on the bone, and call 112.
isole: Immobilise in the position found, blocking the joint above and below (steps in Help reachable mode).
Leg with no sticks to hand: tie it to the other leg, with padding between them.
Arm or wrist: splint, then sling and a bandage strapping the arm to the body. You can often still walk.
Check fingers or toes every hour: warm, pink, with feeling. Loosen the ties if it swells.
Bone visible: rinse the wound thoroughly with drinking water, cover with a clean cloth, don't touch the bone. The risk of infection makes getting out a priority.
Limb badly bent with a cold, pale, numb hand or foot, and no help for hours: pull gently and slowly in line to straighten it, then immobilise. Stop if the pain increases sharply or it won't move.
alerte: Hand or foot cold, pale or numb
Fracture of the thigh or pelvis: risk of major blood loss
ps_attelle.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ERC) cross-checked with manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_brancard.intro: Carrying a casualty is exhausting and risky: only do it if help can't come or the place is dangerous.
etapes: Find two strong poles about 2 m long (sound dead wood, joined walking poles).
Jacket method: zip up 2 or 3 jackets, turn the sleeves inside out and slide the poles through the sleeves.
Tarp method: lay one pole a third of the way across the tarp, fold over, lay the second pole, fold the rest over: the casualty's weight locks the fabric.
Test the stretcher with an uninjured person before putting the casualty on it.
Carry with 4 people if possible (2 are enough on easy ground), walking out of step, and take frequent breaks.
On a slope, keep the casualty's head uphill. Cover them and check their breathing at each break.
attention: Don't move a casualty who may have injured their spine, unless there is immediate danger.
isole: Alone with a casualty: only move them a short distance, to shelter or out of danger.
Drag the casualty lying on a tarp, sleeping bag or jacket, pulling by the shoulders, head towards you.
Over a longer distance: build a travois (two poles in a V joined by crosspieces and a tarp) that you pull by the point.
Take frequent breaks, check breathing and keep the casualty covered.
alerte: Suspected back or neck injury: only move if there is immediate danger
ps_brancard.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ERC) cross-checked with manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_laisser.titre: Leaving a casualty to fetch help
ps_laisser.intro: If nobody can call and you're alone with a casualty, you may have to go and fetch help. Preparing this departure well can save their life.
etapes: First, try everything to call: 112, SMS, climbing to a high point, waiting for someone to pass on the path.
Settle the casualty: sheltered, insulated from the ground, covered (survival blanket, dry clothes), in the recovery position if unconscious.
Leave within reach: water, food, torch, whistle, an extra warm garment.
Note their exact position (GPS coordinates from the crisis button, or precise landmarks) and write it down.
Leave a visible note: time of departure, the casualty's condition, direction taken.
Mark the route (branches, tape) to guide the rescuers back, and head for the nearest place you can call from.
attention: If the group has at least three people: one stays with the casualty, the other two leave together.
isole: Stay with the casualty and signal if they can't be left alone (unconscious, in shock), if night or bad weather is coming, or if you don't know the way.
Go for help if nobody will come looking for you, the casualty is stable and sheltered, and you know the way to somewhere you can call from.
Before leaving: casualty warm, insulated from the ground, with water, food, torch and whistle within reach.
Note their position (the app's crisis button), leave a note with the time of departure and the direction taken, and mark the route.
alerte: Casualty unconscious or in shock: only leave them alone as an absolute last resort
ps_laisser.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ERC) cross-checked with manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

nuit_sans_duvet.titre: Spending the night without a sleeping bag
nuit_sans_duvet.intro: An unplanned night outdoors without a sleeping bag: the aim is not to lose your heat, neither to the ground, nor to the wind, nor to damp.
etapes: Stop before nightfall and before you're exhausted, so you have time to prepare.
Insulate from the ground first: a thick layer (20 to 30 cm compressed) of dead leaves, ferns or fine branches, or your emptied pack.
Get out of the wind: a dip in the ground, a big trunk, a rock, a tarp or branch shelter.
Put on all your dry clothes. Stuff dry leaves into the space between two layers of clothing: they trap air like down.
Wrap yourself in the survival blanket or a big bin bag, head covered.
Eat and drink before sleeping, and move (tense your muscles) whenever the cold wakes you.
Huddle together if there are several of you.
attention: If a fire is possible and allowed: a fire along your body with a reflector wall behind you, at a safe distance from the shelter.
nuit_sans_duvet.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten for Bivaska

chaleur.intro: In summer, heat and sun wear you out faster than cold. Shade and calm are your best allies.
etapes: Walk early in the morning and late in the day, stop in the shade during the hot hours.
Cover your head and neck, wear loose, light-coloured clothing, keep long sleeves against the sun.
Make effective shade: stretch a tarp at least 50 cm off the ground so air can circulate. With two sheets stacked 20 to 30 cm apart, the shade is much cooler.
Don't lie directly on scorching ground: insulate yourself with your pack or branches.
Drink regularly before you're thirsty, and eat salty food.
Wet a scarf or T-shirt: evaporation cools you.
attention: Hot, dry skin, violent headache, confusion: heatstroke, a life-threatening emergency. Shade, water on the skin, fanning, 112.
chaleur.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten for Bivaska
